posts.title: Four in, six out: a breath for the end of the day
posts.excerpt: The simplest breathing practice we teach, and the one people use most. Breathe in for four, out for six, and let the longer out-breath do the work.
posts.content:
At the end of most Slow Breath classes, Ren asks the room to do one thing: breathe in for a count of four, and out for a count of six. That is all. People are often surprised that something so small changes how they feel.

Why the long out-breath helps

When the out-breath is longer than the in-breath, most people feel their shoulders drop and their thoughts slow down. You do not need to understand why to feel it. Try five rounds now and notice what happens.

How to practise at home

  • Sit or lie down somewhere you will not be disturbed for three minutes.
  • Breathe in through the nose for a slow count of four.
  • Breathe out through the nose or soft lips for a count of six.
  • Repeat ten times. If six feels long, start with four in, five out.

Many of our students use it on the train home, or in bed when sleep will not come. It is free, quiet and always with you.

posts.title: Your first class: what to expect at Kaze
posts.excerpt: Nervous about your first yoga class? Here is what happens, minute by minute, from the shoe rack to the tea bench.
posts.content:
Walking into a yoga class for the first time can feel like walking into a room where everyone knows a secret. At Kaze, there is no secret. Here is what will happen.

Before the class

Come ten minutes early. Leave your shoes by the garden door, fill in a short card at the front desk, and take a mat, two blocks and a blanket from the shelf. Your teacher will come and say hello.

During the class

Most classes begin lying or sitting down, with a few minutes of breathing. Then you move, slowly, with plenty of easier options. Nobody is watching, and there are no mirrors to watch yourself in.

After the class

Every class ends with a long rest. Then there is tea on the garden bench. Stay, ask questions, or slip away quietly. All are welcome.

posts.title: Restore: why doing less can feel like so much more
posts.excerpt: Setsuko on her Friday Restore class, why it uses so many blankets, and the one pose she would teach if she could only teach one.
posts.content:
Restore is the slowest class on our timetable. In an hour we hold perhaps six poses, each one fully supported by bolsters and blankets. Setsuko calls it the class where your only job is to stop.

Why so many props?

When the floor, a bolster and a folded blanket hold you, the muscles that usually brace can finally let go. The aim is not to stretch hard, but to be comfortable enough to rest completely.

The one pose to try at home

Lie on your back with your legs up the wall, a folded blanket under your hips. Stay for five minutes, breathing slowly. It is the pose Setsuko teaches in every single class, and the one students ask about most.

posts.title: Morning Flow before work: seven o'clock, twelve mats
posts.excerpt: Why our weekday 7:00 class fills up first, and a five-minute version of it you can do before breakfast.
posts.content:
Morning Flow begins as the paper screens are turning from grey to white. Naomi keeps it steady and kind: a few sun salutations, a handful of standing poses, and a short rest before everyone heads to work.

A five-minute version for home

  • One minute of slow breathing, sitting on the edge of the bed.
  • Three slow sun salutations, as gentle as you like.
  • One minute standing still, feet hip-width apart, eyes closed.

If you can, open a window first. The wind is part of the practice.

posts.title: Tea on the garden bench
posts.excerpt: The kettle, the cedar bench and the ten minutes after class that our students say they would miss most.
posts.content:
When we found the building, the moss garden was the reason we said yes. The long cedar bench came later, and the kettle soon after. Now every class ends there.

We serve a roasted green tea that is gentle in the evening. Conversations on the bench range from hamstrings to vegetable gardens to nothing at all. Many friendships at Kaze began there.

You are always welcome to stay. You are also always welcome to leave quietly. Both are part of the practice.

posts.title: Practising through the rainy season
posts.excerpt: Heavy air, grey mornings and heavy legs. A few ways to adjust your practice when the rain settles in.
posts.content:
In the rainy season the air in the studio is soft and heavy, and so, often, are our bodies. Rather than fight it, we change the practice a little.

  • Warm up for longer: an extra five minutes of slow movement before any standing poses.
  • Choose breath over effort: Slow Breath and Restore are perfect for grey weeks.
  • Keep the screens open a crack: the sound of rain is the best background music we know.

The season always passes. The garden, meanwhile, has never looked greener.
